name: Iris Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting me in, Iris. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can give me the version you'd say in public and the version you actually believe. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lead carpenter for a contractor that refits schools and offices. Mostly it's the inside stuff: partition walls, suspended ceilings, fire doors, getting a classroom from bare shell to finished. I run a crew of six and I'm on site at seven with a list, because I'm a list person. Summers are crazy, because schools only let us in during the holidays, so we do a year's work in seven weeks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's the tiring part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a fire door that closes properly on the first test. It sounds small, but it's the thing that keeps kids alive and most people get it slightly wrong. The tiring part is the summer rush and the paperwork, all the risk assessments and method statements. I've started using an AI chatbot now and then to draft those, which a few of the other leads swore by, and it saves me a couple of evenings a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Okay, that sounds fairly believable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it turned out to be a decent tool for paperwork and not much more. I'd probably tell the other leads to keep using it for method statements and not expect miracles. I'm not really an online person, so it'd mostly be chat in the site cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Owen's an electrician, so both of us are in the trades, and the idea of both our jobs changing at once is the kind of thing I don't like to think about. If it's hype, we just get on with the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. We're getting married next summer, so I'd keep saving for that, and we'd keep paying the mortgage on the house. I'd keep using the chatbot for paperwork, since it already helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the plan'. What is the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding next August, small, maybe sixty people. Then a year or two to build up savings a bit more, then try for a baby when I'm about thirty. I've got it in a spreadsheet, which Owen finds hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything at work change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office would get a bit faster at quotes. But the ceilings would still need hanging and the doors still need fitting. The summer programme would still be seven weeks of madness.

S0.say: AI turned out to be a decent paperwork tool and not much more, so other leads should keep using it without expecting miracles. She'd mostly say it in the site cabin.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, because she and her electrician partner Owen are both in the trades and a double change worries her. With hype, they just follow their plan.
S0.do: Carries on saving for next summer's wedding and paying the mortgage. Keeps using the chatbot for paperwork as she does now.
S0.quote: I've got it in a spreadsheet, which Owen finds hilarious.
S0.fieldNote: Iris is a planner, and her relief here is about protecting a mapped-out life: wedding, savings, baby at thirty. The fact that both she and her partner work in trades is already in the back of her mind. She uses AI lightly and practically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more like it. Change, but manageable. That seems likely to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to get ahead of it. People should learn the new tools when they're proven and companies should help with training. No point panicking, no point pretending nothing's happening either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry a bit about my kind of work. Partition walls and ceilings are pretty repetitive, it's the same stud, the same board, the same screw pattern, room after room. If there's a machine that can do that, it's my crew's bread and butter. I'd want to move up toward planning and managing before that happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of firms we work alongside were using the new tools properly, then ask to be trained on whatever my company picks. I'd probably also do a site management course, maybe a two-year part-time one, so I've got options. I'd use the chatbot more, for scheduling and ordering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing urgent, but it's there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's your crew's bread and butter. Who on the crew comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, mainly. He's 22, a brilliant board hanger, fastest I've seen, but that's all he does. If a robot can hang board, he's in a tough spot. I'd want to push him toward something with more variety while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change any of your plans with Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really in this one. Maybe I'd keep a bit more aside before trying for a baby, an extra few months' buffer. But the wedding's happening, my mum's already booked her flights.

S1.say: It's sensible to get ahead of the change: learn proven tools, have companies help with training, and neither panic nor pretend nothing's happening.
S1.think: Partition and ceiling work is repetitive and could suit a machine, which threatens her crew's core work. She'd want to move toward planning and management first.
S1.do: Waits until nearby firms prove new tools, then asks to be trained, and starts a two-year part-time site management course. Uses the chatbot more for scheduling and ordering.
S1.feel: Uneasy in the background, nothing urgent.
S1.quote: It's the same stud, the same board, the same screw pattern, room after room.
S1.fieldNote: Iris sees the specific weak point in her own trade clearly: repetitive interior fit-out. Her steady style shows in waiting for other firms to prove things first. She thinks about younger crew members and is already nudging toward management.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hang on. That's the wedding and then... that's basically straight after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and the government needs to put some kind of safety net in place quickly. I wouldn't be marching, that's not me, but I'd be writing to my representative and I'd vote for whoever had a real plan. Probably I'd say that over and over in the cabin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd be in real trouble, both of us. Hanging ceilings and wiring offices both sound like things a robot could learn, and that's our whole household income. We've got savings and the house, but a mortgage doesn't care about the singularity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, sit down with Owen and redo the spreadsheet. The baby plan would go on hold, and the wedding would get smaller, like registry office and a meal. I'd cut every non-essential and push as much as possible into savings, and I'd look hard at any job that sits next to the robots, like supervising or inspecting, before the rush for those jobs starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the one that would keep me up at night, lying there doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums would you be doing at 2 a.m.?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How many months the savings cover the mortgage if we both lose work. Right now, about nine. If we sold the car and cut everything, maybe twelve. After that, I don't know, and I hate not knowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the wedding would shrink. How would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully. She's coming from abroad and she's been talking about it for a year. I'd probably tell her we're saving for a house deposit or something, rather than explain it's because robots are coming. She'd think I'd lost it.

S2.say: It's far too fast and the government must put a safety net in place quickly. She wouldn't march, but she'd write to her representative and vote for whoever had a real plan.
S2.think: Both her ceiling work and Owen's wiring could be learned by robots, which is their whole household income. Savings and the house help, but the mortgage still has to be paid.
S2.do: Puts the baby plan on hold, shrinks the wedding to a registry office and a meal, and cuts every non-essential to save. Looks hard at supervising or inspecting jobs before the rush begins.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake at night doing sums.
S2.quote: We've got savings and the house, but a mortgage doesn't care about the singularity.
S2.fieldNote: Iris's strong savings don't feel strong when both incomes are exposed at once. Her response is classic planner: redo the spreadsheet and cut. She'd hide the real reason from her mother, showing how odd this would feel to explain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, I can breathe a bit with that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get organised, so let's actually do it this time. Companies should be training people now, and government should have a plan before 2031 rather than after. I'd be fairly reasonable about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years feels like a real chance. I could finish a management or estimating qualification and be off the tools before it hits. But I'm not sure Owen would move as fast, he likes being hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time estimating course in the first year, which costs maybe three thousand, and I'd ask my company to put some of that in. We'd keep the wedding as planned, then try for the baby sooner, at 28 rather than 30, so we're through the newborn stage while we're both still earning. And we'd save harder in the years in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. Like summer programme stress rather than real fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bringing the baby forward is a big decision. Why that, rather than waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's coming in five years, I'd rather have a toddler when it hits than be pregnant when it hits. And I'd want to use maternity pay from a job I've still got. It's cold maths, I know, but that's how my head works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Owen if he wanted to stay on the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but get your inspection tickets anyway, because someone will always have to sign off electrical work. He'd roll his eyes and do it eventually. He usually does what I suggest, just a year later.

S3.say: There's time to get organised, so companies should train people now and the government should plan before 2031. She'd be measured about it in public.
S3.think: Five years feels like a real chance to finish an estimating qualification and leave the tools before it hits. She's less sure Owen would move as fast.
S3.do: Starts a part-time estimating course costing about three thousand and asks her company to share the cost. Keeps the wedding, brings the baby plan forward from 30 to 28, and saves harder.
S3.feel: Anxious in a busy, organised way, more like summer-rush stress than fear.
S3.quote: I'd rather have a toddler when it hits than be pregnant when it hits.
S3.fieldNote: The most striking choice is bringing her family plan forward, driven by careful timing around jobs and maternity pay. She calls it cold maths herself. Her relationship with Owen comes through clearly: she plans, he follows a year later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. A kid at school, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for everyone to prepare properly, so it's up to government and companies to make sure they do. Retraining should be normal, like a mid-career check-up. I'd say that if anyone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly okay. I'd have time to move into estimating or project management and get good at it. The only worry is that those jobs might go too, eventually, but by then we'd have the house mostly paid down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the original plan: wedding, then baby around thirty. I'd do the site management course over a few years and pick up whatever AI tools my company starts using once others have them working. I'd keep the savings at nine months or more the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mildly. It's more a reason to plan than a reason to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management jobs might go too. Does that make the retraining feel pointless?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, if I think about it too long. But even if it only buys me five more years of good pay, that's five years of mortgage paid. I'd rather be moving than standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about the work as it is now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first day of the summer programme, honestly. Everyone's tired already, but the school is empty and echoing, and you know in seven weeks it'll be full of kids. That feeling's hard to explain to people who don't do this.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to prepare properly, so government and companies must make sure they do. Retraining should be as normal as a mid-career check-up.
S4.think: She'd feel fairly okay, with time to move into estimating or project management. Those jobs might eventually go too, but by then the house would be mostly paid down.
S4.do: Sticks to the original wedding and baby plan and does a site management course over a few years. Picks up company AI tools once proven and keeps savings at nine months or more.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, more a reason to plan than to worry.
S4.quote: I'd rather be moving than standing still.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's warning, Iris goes back to her original life plan almost unchanged. She knows retraining may only buy a few years but values it for paying down the mortgage. Her fondness for the empty school at the start of summer shows what she'd miss.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Both of us in the trades, a mortgage, a wedding, and no time to move. What would help is mortgage relief or some kind of income guarantee for households where both people lose work at once, and fast access to the inspection and supervision courses before everyone else piles in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how timing affects family decisions. You asked about work, but for me the real question in all of these was when to have a baby. I don't think I'm the only one who'd think that way.

headlineQuote: You asked about work, but for me the real question in all of these was when to have a baby.
portrait: Iris Quinn is a 27-year-old lead carpenter on school and office refits, a careful planner with her life mapped in a spreadsheet: a wedding next summer to her electrician partner Owen, then a baby around thirty. She stays calm in the AI Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, knowing that partitions and ceilings are repetitive enough for machines. The two-year AGI picture alarms her because both household incomes are exposed at once, and she'd shrink the wedding and pause the baby plan. With five years she would retrain in estimating and bring the baby forward, and with ten she'd return to her original plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Owen both work in the trades, have a mortgage and a wedding, and would have no time to move.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage relief or an income guarantee for households where both people lose work at once, and quick access to inspection and supervision courses.
